episode.throughLine: A child's remembered family care and exclusion from play; an incomplete primary-source record does not yet establish a publishable recovery arc.

contentProfile.contentNote: Childhood polio, mobility aids, teasing and exclusion. Includes historical removal of braces, not medical advice or a model for readers.

facts.statement: Wilma Rudolph became an Olympic sprinter and won three gold medals at the 1960 Games.

arc.canonicalText:
A girl's care involved her brothers and sisters as well as adults. She later remembered wearing leg braces until about nine. Members of her family went to hospital with her to learn how to help.

The care continued at home.
arc.sourceNote: SOURCE/CRAFT HOLD: first-person interview is represented by an explicitly unverified and visibly garbled transcript, not a soundtrack audit. This is a recurring care situation, not a located encounter. About nine is memory-framed and disputed, not a settled medical chronology.

arc.canonicalText:
She remembered being teased by other children. She also remembered not being accepted into their play. That exclusion was difficult for her.

She wanted to play.
arc.sourceNote: SOURCE/CRAFT HOLD: testimony supports hurt and exclusion, but not a particular playground, child, day, insult or single lowest encounter. No invented scene or private despair.

arc.canonicalText: At home, she took off her braces with help from her siblings. In her account, her father was protective and reluctant to let her remove them. The children helped without telling him.
arc.sourceNote: SOURCE HOLD: this passage paraphrases a damaged transcript segment and needs soundtrack or authoritative transcript verification before acceptance. No procedural detail is supplied. This is historical conduct, not advice to remove medical equipment or conceal care decisions.

arc.canonicalText:
The need for help had affected more than play. She remembered missing her first two years of school. She had a teacher at home.

Care also involved the hospital visits her family shared. At home, they repeated what they had learned. Her mother remained positive about her walking.
arc.sourceNote: SOURCE/CRAFT HOLD: this establishes extended care and interrupted schooling, not a located failed attempt or reversal. No falls, painful practice, failed treatment or exact therapy schedule have been invented.

arc.canonicalText: In her later account, she eventually stopped wearing the braces. She placed that change at about nine. She no longer wore them.
arc.sourceNote: SOURCE/CRAFT HOLD: age is disputed and no directly accessed primary account supplies the purported church walk or doctor-office demonstration. This is a remembered change of condition, not an attested single turning day. A real located trigger and next action are still missing.

arc.canonicalText:
Around thirteen, she remembered discovering that girls could take part in sports. Her older sister played basketball. Basketball was her own first sport.

Her childhood account also stressed the people who had expected her to walk. She remembered their confidence.
arc.sourceNote: Childhood endpoint only; no Olympic victory presented as medical repayment. SOURCE/CRAFT HOLD: basketball is a later remembered condition, not an immediate or proven result of removing braces.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Wilma Rudolph. She became an Olympic sprint champion. Your life is not theirs.

But a piece of this story may still sit beside you. You are allowed to need help.
arc.sourceNote: No approval. Source verification, complete arc evidence and owner reading remain required. Readers who use mobility aids are not asked to reject them.

dramatizationLimits: SOURCE HOLD: unverified transcript has substantial recognition errors; no claim that the soundtrack or authoritative transcript was audited.
CRAFT HOLD: located scene, lowest moment, failed effort and causal turning encounter are missing.
Do not invent church or clinic walking scenes, falls, sensations, dialogue, therapy instructions or prognosis.
Dates preserve the installed 1945–1953 stage; ages 5–13 follow the 1940 birth year rather than installed matching ages 8–16. Exact brace chronology remains disputed.
avoidRules: No miracle cure, medical advice, mind-over-body moral or claim that effort determines disability outcomes.
No instruction to remove braces, conceal medical decisions or reject professional care.
Do not use the familiar doctor-versus-mother quotation without its original record; accessed interview gives a more complicated account.
Do not imply that support is deserved only when it produces exceptional achievement.
No matching, runtime or production changes; no reader-disclosure echo or outcome promise.

sources.citation: Wilma Rudolph, Black Champions interview, April 11, 1985; William Miles collection, Washington University Film & Media Archive, via AAPB. Accessed unverified computer/third-party transcript, not an audited soundtrack.
